column1: # title: ENG-205 Beowulf Part 1 — 4 Main Ideas
How Shield Sheafson founded the Danish line
column2: Shield Sheafson arrived as an abandoned child, grew into a conqueror who made neighboring clans pay tribute, and founded the Danish royal line.
The Danes laid Shield in a ship heaped with treasure and set it adrift, sending him back to the sea that had first brought him.

column1: What a young prince should do
column2: The poet teaches that a young prince should give gifts freely so that loyal companions will stand beside him when war comes.
Hrothgar's success in war drew a large army of followers, so he built Heorot as a great hall where he could share treasure with them.
The poet warns that Heorot will one day burn in a feud between in-laws, which casts a shadow over the new hall.
Grendel, an outcast from God, is tormented by the joyful noise of feasting and the scop's song of creation, so he attacks the hall.
Grendel crept into Heorot after a feast, seized thirty sleeping warriors, and carried their bodies back to his lair.
Grendel's repeated raids forced the Danes to sleep elsewhere, so the greatest hall in the world stood empty after dark.

column1: Why Grendel's feud cannot be settled
column2: Grendel refused to make peace or pay the death-price, so the Danes could not end his feud in the normal way.

column1: Why the Danes pray to idols
column2: In despair the Danes made offerings at pagan shrines, which the Christian narrator condemns because they did not know the true God.

column1: How Beowulf decides to go to Denmark
column2: When Beowulf heard of Grendel, he ordered a ship and chose the best men he could find, and the Geat elders encouraged him after reading good omens.
The Geats' ship flew over the waves "like a bird," and they reached the Danish cliffs the next day and thanked God for the easy crossing.
The Danish coast-guard rode down to the armed strangers, demanded to know who they were, and let them pass once Beowulf explained his errand.

column1: How the Geats are received at Heorot
column2: Wulfgar questioned the Geats at the door and reported to Hrothgar, who recognized Beowulf as Ecgtheow's son and welcomed them.
Beowulf asked for the privilege of cleansing Heorot with only his own men and vowed to fight Grendel without sword or shield.
Because Grendel uses no weapons, Beowulf gives up his own to make the fight equal and to raise Hygelac's fame.
Beowulf asks that his mail shirt be sent back to Hygelac if he dies, since Grendel would leave no body to bury.
Unferth, jealous of Beowulf's fame, claims that Beowulf lost a reckless swimming contest to Breca and will lose to Grendel too.
Beowulf says that beer is doing Unferth's talking, retells the swim as a victory over sea monsters, and shames Unferth for killing his brothers and failing to stop Grendel.
Wealhtheow passed the mead cup first to Hrothgar and then down the ranks, and when she reached Beowulf he vowed to succeed or die in the hall.
Hrothgar entrusted Heorot to Beowulf for the night, the first time he had ever given control of the hall to anyone else.

column1: What happens in the section The Fight with Grendel
column2: Grendel burst into Heorot and ate a sleeping Geat, but when he reached for Beowulf, Beowulf locked his hand in an unbreakable grip.
Beowulf held Grendel's hand until the sinews split and the arm tore off at the shoulder, so Grendel fled to his mere to die.

column1: Why the Geats' swords fail against Grendel
column2: Beowulf's men struck at Grendel with their swords, but a spell kept any blade from harming him.
The struggle tore the mead-benches from the floor and the doors from their hinges, and only the roof was left undamaged.
Beowulf displayed Grendel's whole arm and shoulder high under Heorot's roof as proof that he had fulfilled his boast.
Warriors followed Grendel's bloody tracks to the mere, where the water boiled with gore, and rode back praising Beowulf.

column1: The scop's song of Sigemund and Heremod
column2: On the ride back a poet praised Beowulf by comparing him to the dragon-slayer Sigemund and contrasting him with the cruel king Heremod.
Hrothgar thanked God for the victory and declared that he now loved Beowulf as a son and would deny him nothing.
Beowulf tells Hrothgar he wishes he had held Grendel until he died in the hall, but God let the monster slip away and leave his arm behind.
Unferth boasted less once the hall saw Grendel's steel-hard claw hanging under the eaves.
At a great feast Hrothgar gave Beowulf a golden standard, a helmet, a mail shirt, a sword, and eight horses, and he paid gold for the Geat whom Grendel had eaten.
The scop sang of a Danish-Frisian feud in which a forced truce between Hengest and Finn broke into revenge and Finn was killed.
The Finn story shows that revenge breaks every forced peace, which foreshadows the feuds that will later destroy the Danes.
The Finn story shows how women suffer in feuds, since Hildeburh loses her brother and her son, who fought on opposite sides.
Wealhtheow reminds Hrothgar to leave the throne to his own kin rather than to Beowulf, whom he has just adopted as a son.
When Wealhtheow gives Beowulf the torque, the poet foretells that Hygelac will wear it when he dies raiding the Frisians.
The Danes slept in Heorot with their weapons at hand, not knowing that one of them was already marked for death.
Beowulf's boasts, Hrothgar's gifts, and the Geats' loyalty show a world in which courage is repaid with treasure and fame.
A boast was a public promise, so Beowulf's boasts bind him to act, and his victory over Grendel proves them true.
Beowulf says "fate goes ever as fate must," yet the narrator insists that God decides the outcome, which blends pagan fate with Christian providence.
The Christian narrator links Grendel to Cain and praises God, while the characters live by the pagan customs of feud, boast, and treasure.
A lord's gifts publicly show his gratitude and bind his warriors to him, so treasure measures both honor and loyalty.
Ecgtheow's feud, Grendel's endless raids, and the Finn story all show that every killing demands revenge or payment.
The narrator reminds listeners that every soul must reach its appointed deathbed, so fame is the only reward that lasts.
Heorot's gold, light, and song stand for human civilization, while Grendel comes out of the dark fens as its enemy.
